title: Oracles on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, and Elam
summary: Jeremiah's oracles against the nations continue with five peoples: Ammon, which had seized Israelite land; Edom, proud of its wisdom and its mountain strongholds; Damascus and the Aramean cities to the north; the desert tribes of Kedar and Hazor, whom Nebuchadnezzar would raid; and distant Elam in the east. Each will fall, yet the chapter also promises that God will restore the fortunes of Ammon and Elam.
story: Chapters 46 to 51 gather Jeremiah's oracles against the nations, fulfilling his call to be a prophet to the nations (1:5, 10). Egypt, Philistia, and Moab have been addressed in chapters 46 to 48; this chapter takes up the rest of Judah's neighbors before the long climax against Babylon in chapters 50 and 51. Behind the list stands the vision of the cup of wrath in 25:15-29, where the prophet is told to make the nations drink from the LORD's cup, starting with Jerusalem. The message to Judah's readers is double. Their own suffering was not the end of God's justice, since every nation that trusted in its riches or heights would be judged by the same God. And the God who judges is not merely Israel's tribal deity: he disposes of the thrones of Elam as surely as those of Judah, and he can promise mercy even beyond Israel.
historical:
The peoples named here surrounded Judah on the east and north. Ammon lay east of the Jordan around its capital Rabbah (modern Amman). After the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III deported the Israelite tribes east of the Jordan in the 730s BC (1 Chronicles 5:26), Ammon moved into the territory of Gad, which is the grievance behind verse 1. Ammon also played a part in Judah's last days: its king Baalis sponsored the murder of the governor Gedaliah (40:14). Edom lay south and east of the Dead Sea, with Bozrah as a major city and Teman as a region or town famous for its wise men. Dedan was an oasis in northwestern Arabia whose caravans traded through Edom. Edom's conduct when Jerusalem fell (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10-14) left a bitter memory, and in later centuries Arab peoples pressed into Edom's land while Edomites moved into southern Judah, the region later called Idumea.

Damascus, Hamath, and Arpad were Aramean (Syrian) cities that had already been crushed by Assyria in the eighth century BC; the oracle may draw on older language, and Ben-hadad was the name of several earlier kings of Damascus. Kedar was a powerful Arab tribal confederation of the Syrian desert, and the kingdoms of Hazor here are not the Galilean city of that name but desert settlements. The Babylonian Chronicle, a series of cuneiform tablets recording events year by year, reports that Nebuchadnezzar raided the Arabs of the desert in his sixth year (about 599/598 BC), which fits verses 28 to 33. Elam lay far to the east, in what is now southwestern Iran, with its capital at Susa. The Elam oracle is dated to the beginning of Zedekiah's reign, about 597 BC; Elam was later absorbed into the Persian Empire, and Susa became one of the Persian royal cities.
cultural:
Each oracle speaks to the thing its nation trusted. Ammon trusted its fruitful valleys and riches, and its god Milcom (called Molech in some passages, and named as the detestable god of the Ammonites in 1 Kings 11:5). The prophecy that Milcom will go into exile along with his priests reflects the ancient practice of conquerors carrying off the statues of defeated gods as trophies. Edom trusted its wisdom and its geography. Its heartland was a rugged plateau of sandstone cliffs, and its people lived, as verse 16 says, in the clefts of the rocks and on mountain summits, strongholds that seemed beyond reach. Israel remembered Edom as descended from Esau, Jacob's brother, which is why the oracle calls him Esau and why his betrayal cut so deep.

The desert tribes of Kedar lived in tents, kept camels and flocks, and had no walled cities: they had no gates or bars and lived alone (verse 31). Their security was distance and mobility, not stone. Verse 32 describes them as those who shave their temples, an Arab custom of cutting the hair at the sides that the Greek historian Herodotus also describes and that Israelite law forbade for Israel (Leviticus 19:27). Elam was famed for its archers, so the oracle strikes at exactly that point: God will shatter Elam's bow. The image of drinking the cup (verse 12) drew on a familiar picture of a host handing a guest a drink he cannot refuse; here the drink is judgment.
literary: The chapter is a sequence of five separate poems, each with its own heading (verses 1, 7, 23, 28, and 34), much like the headed oracles of Isaiah 13 to 23 and Amos 1 and 2. The poems use rhetorical questions (Has Israel no sons? Is there no longer wisdom in Teman?), mock laments that summon the victims to wail, and vivid images of predators: a lion from the Jordan's thickets, an eagle spreading its wings. Much of the Edom poem closely parallels the short book of Obadiah: verses 9 and 10 match Obadiah 5 and 6, and verses 14 to 16 match Obadiah 1 to 4. Scholars debate whether one prophet drew on the other or both drew on a common oracle. Verses 19 to 21 reappear almost word for word against Babylon in 50:44-46, a sign that Jeremiah's oracles were shaped as a collection. The Elam oracle alone carries a date and ends the chapter with a promise for the last days.

outline.t: Ammon: the seizure of Gad avenged, and a promise of restoration
Edom: no gleanings left, and the cup that must be drunk
Edom: the eagle's nest brought down
Damascus, Hamath, and Arpad in panic
Kedar and Hazor: the tent peoples plundered
Elam: the bow broken, the throne replaced, the future restored

doctrines.note: The LORD disposes of every nation on the map, from Judah's next-door neighbors to distant Elam. He says, “I will set My throne in Elam” (verse 38). Kings and gods who seemed secure answer to him.

Judgment falls on specific sins: land-grabbing, arrogance, trust in wealth and height. The logic of verse 12 is that if even the less deserving must drink the cup, the proud cannot expect to be spared. God's justice is not favoritism toward Israel; it is one standard for all.
Oracles of doom end, for Ammon and Elam, with a promise: “Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity” (verse 39). God's purposes for the nations are not exhausted by judgment.

words.note: Kos, cup. An ordinary drinking vessel that the prophets turned into a symbol of what God gives someone to experience, often his wrath (Jeremiah 25:15; Isaiah 51:17). Here it means that Edom cannot escape the judgment that other nations must swallow. The image stands behind Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane that the cup might pass from him.

Chokmah, wisdom. In the Old Testament the word covers skill, practical good sense, and the art of living well under God. Edom was known for it: Job's friend Eliphaz came from Teman. The taunt of verse 7 is that wisdom cut off from God cannot see disaster coming.

Zadon, arrogance or presumption, the pride that overreaches. Verse 16 says it has deceived Edom. In Proverbs this pride comes before a fall; in Edom's case it is linked to physical height, a nest among the crags that felt out of reach of anyone, including God.

Shevut, captivity or fortunes. The phrase translated restore from captivity can mean both bringing back exiles and reversing someone's fortunes generally. Jeremiah uses it for Israel's future (30:3) and here, remarkably, for Ammon (verse 6) and Elam (verse 39).

christ: The chapter does not predict Christ, but two of its threads run toward him. The first is the cup. The prophets pictured judgment as a cup the nations must drink; in Gethsemane Jesus asked that this cup pass from him, and then drank it, taking up the judgment the prophets had announced. The second is the promise to Elam. On the day of Pentecost, Luke lists Elamites among the crowd who heard the apostles speak of God's mighty works in their own languages (Acts 2:9). That is not a hidden fulfillment code, but it shows the direction of the story: the God who promised to restore the fortunes of a distant, pagan people gathers the nations into his kingdom through the risen Christ.

hard.q: Why does God promise restoration to Ammon and Elam but not to Edom?
hard.a: The chapter treats the nations differently. Ammon (verse 6) and Elam (verse 39), like Egypt (46:26) and Moab (48:47), receive a promise that their fortunes will be restored, while Edom's desolation is described as lasting forever (verse 13). Some readers see this as a reflection of Edom's particular guilt, especially its violence against its brother Judah in the day of Jerusalem's fall, which the prophets remembered with special grief. Others note that Old Testament language about perpetual ruin often describes a nation's political end, which did come for Edom as a kingdom, rather than the fate of every individual descended from it. Still others point out that the prophets elsewhere foresee even Edom's remnant brought under David's rule (Amos 9:12, cited in Acts 15:17 as including the nations). The fair conclusion is that the chapter speaks of peoples as political bodies in history, and it does not settle the eternal destiny of individuals.

questions: Edom trusted its wisdom and its heights. What are the heights you or your community rely on to feel beyond the reach of trouble?
Ammon took advantage of Israel's weakness to seize land. Where are you tempted to profit from another person's misfortune?
What does it mean for your view of God that he promises a future even to Elam, a distant people with no covenant claim on him?
